name: Does converting PDF to JPG upload my file?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. PDFree converts PDF pages to images entirely in your browser using PDF.js (Mozilla's open-source PDF renderer). Nothing is uploaded to any server. You can verify this: open DevTools → Network tab and you should not see your PDF being uploaded during conversion.

name: What image quality can I expect?

acceptedAnswer.text: PDFree renders PDF pages at 72, 150, or 300 DPI. At 300 DPI the output is print quality — text is sharp and readable at any zoom. At 150 DPI the images are clear for screen use and most office applications.

name: Can I convert PDF to PNG instead of JPG?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. PDFree supports both JPG and PNG output. PNG is lossless and better for text-heavy documents or charts where you need pixel-perfect sharpness. JPG produces smaller files and is better for photo-heavy pages. Select the format before converting.

name: Can I convert only specific pages to JPG?

acceptedAnswer.text: The tool currently converts all pages at once. To export only specific pages, first use the PDFree Split PDF tool to extract the pages you need into a separate PDF, then convert that PDF to JPG. Both steps are free and run locally in your browser.

name: Will a 10-page PDF produce 10 separate JPG files?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Each page becomes one JPG or PNG file. If your PDF has more than one page, all images are bundled into a ZIP archive for download in one click.

name: Is there a page limit for conversion?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. There are no page count or file size limits. Very large PDFs (100+ pages at 300 DPI) may take longer to process. For best results with large files, close other browser tabs before converting.

name: Is the PDF to JPG converter completely free?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. PDFree is free with no subscription, no signup, and no watermarks on the output. There are no daily limits or file size restrictions.

name: What is the maximum output resolution?

acceptedAnswer.text: PDFree exports up to 300 DPI, which is standard print-quality resolution. PDF text and vector graphics render sharply at 300 DPI — the output looks identical to the original document.
